mainTopic: Measuring צער, the rules of ריפוי and a reopened wound, and paying the other payments along with נזק
overview: This amud finishes the מחלוקת between רבי and בן עזאי about whether a כלל ופרט still works when other words separate the two terms. It explains why רבי still needs the word חבורה. The גמרא then asks how to measure צער when there is also נזק. After several attempts, it settles on what a person would pay to have a hand that the government already condemned removed by a painless drug instead of a sword. Next comes ריפוי. A ברייתא gives three views on a wound that reopens, and רבה explains the dispute through the rules of bandaging and the doubled phrase ורפא ירפא, which also teaches that a doctor may heal. The גמרא then lists practical rules about which kind of medical care each side may refuse. Last, a ברייתא says all the payments are added on top of נזק, and רב זביד brings the source פצע תחת פצע. A challenge to that source begins at the end of the amud and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The core of the disagreement: a general and specific term that are far apart
steps.stepSummary: רבי and בן עזאי argue about whether we apply כלל ופרט when the two terms are separated by other words.
steps.simpleTranslation: They argue about a general term and a specific term that are far from each other. רבי holds we do not interpret the פסוק with the rule of כלל ופרט. בן עזאי holds we do.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its earlier question, "what are they really arguing about?" It shows that the whole מחלוקת comes down to one rule of reading the תורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the פסוק, כויה (a burn) is the general term at the start, and חבורה (a bruise) is the specific term at the end. פצע sits between them. For רבי, the gap breaks the כלל ופרט, so a burn makes the person liable for צער even without a bruise. For בן עזאי, the כלל ופרט still applies, so the burn must come with a bruise.

keyTerms.meaning: A general term followed by a specific term; the law is limited to the specific case
That are far from each other (separated by other words)

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a practical money question (do you pay for pain from a burn with no bruise?) can depend on a rule for reading פסוקים.

phrases.aramaic: בִּכְלָל וּפְרָט הַמְרוּחָקִים זֶה מִזֶּה קָמִיפַּלְגִי –
phrases.english: They disagree about a general term and a specific term that are far from each other
phrases.notes: שמות 21:25 says כויה first and חבורה last, with פצע in between.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי סָבַר: אֵין דָּנִין אוֹתוֹ בִּכְלָל וּפְרָט,
phrases.english: רבי holds: we do not interpret it with the rule of general and specific,

phrases.aramaic: וּבֶן עַזַּאי סָבַר: דָּנִין אוֹתוֹ בִּכְלָל וּפְרָט.
phrases.english: and בן עזאי holds: we do interpret it with the rule of general and specific.

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּכְלָל וּפְרָט הַמְרוּחָקִים זֶה מִזֶּה קָמִיפַּלְגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from the previous section about the root of the מחלוקת between רבי and בן עזאי
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They disagree about whether a כלל ופרט still applies when the two terms are separated by other words

steps.title: Why does רבי need the word חבורה?
steps.stepSummary: If רבי reads כויה as covering every burn, the word חבורה seems extra.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you will say: according to רבי, why do I need the word חבורה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a problem for רבי's view. If he does not use the word חבורה to limit the law, what is the word there for?
steps.deeperAnalysis: For בן עזאי, חבורה has a clear job: it limits כויה to a burn that comes with a bruise. רבי does not use it that way. A burn with a bruise is already included in כויה, so the word looks useless.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you will say (introduces an expected objection)
A bruise / wound where blood gathers under the skin

phrases.english: And if you will say
according to רבי, why do I need "חבורה"?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא ״חַבּוּרָה״ לְרַבִּי לְמָה לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי's side of the מחלוקת from step 1
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי's reading, which does not use חבורה to limit כויה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Every word in the תורה must teach something. If חבורה adds nothing for רבי, his reading seems to leave it with no job.

steps.title: חבורה teaches extra payment
steps.stepSummary: For רבי, חבורה teaches that a burn with a bruise brings additional payment.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed for additional money.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. For רבי, the word חבורה has its own job: it adds more payment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone who causes a burn that also bruises pays more than for a burn alone. So חבורה is not extra; it raises the amount instead of limiting the case. Both words now teach something for רבי.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי: any burn brings payment for צער, and חבורה adds extra payment. בן עזאי: only a burn with a bruise brings payment for צער, because of כלל ופרט.

phrases.english: For additional money.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְדָמִים יְתֵרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 2
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives the extra word a different job
steps.terutzHavaAmina: חבורה seemed to have no purpose for רבי
steps.terutzMaskana: חבורה teaches that a burn with a bruise brings additional payment

steps.title: Quoting the משנה on how pain is measured
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: we estimate how much a person like this would want to be paid to suffer this pain.
steps.simpleTranslation: We estimate how much a person like this one would want to take, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic by quoting the משנה's method for measuring צער. This is a setup line; the question about it comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Pain cannot be seen or priced directly. So the משנה measures it by asking how much money a similar person would accept to go through the same pain. The words "a person like this one" mean we consider how sensitive this kind of person is to pain.

keyTerms.meaning: Like this one (similar to the victim)
Etc.; the rest of the quote is assumed

phrases.english: We estimate how much a person
like this one would want to take, etc.
phrases.notes: The rest of the משנה says: to be made to suffer like this.

steps.triggerLanguage: אוֹמְדִין כַּמָּה אָדָם כַּיּוֹצֵא בָּזֶה רוֹצֶה לִיטּוֹל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: the method of measuring צער
steps.mimraCoreRuling: צער is measured by how much a similar person would accept to suffer that pain

steps.title: How do we measure pain when there is also damage?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how to price צער alone when the injury also caused נזק.
steps.simpleTranslation: Pain in a case where there is damage: how do we measure it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a practical question about the משנה's method. When a body part is damaged, how do we separate the pain from the damage?
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a plain burn there is only pain, so the estimate is simple. When a limb is also hurt or lost, the person already pays for נזק separately. We need a way to measure only the pain, so we do not charge twice.

keyTerms.meaning: Pain, one of the five payments
Where there is also damage (loss of a body part)

phrases.english: Pain in a case where there is damage,
how do we estimate it?

steps.triggerLanguage: צַעַר בִּמְקוֹם נֶזֶק הֵיכִי שָׁיְימִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how to apply the משנה quoted in step 4 to a harder case
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A method to measure pain alone when there is also physical damage

steps.title: אבוה דשמואל: what would someone take to have his hand cut off?
steps.stepSummary: אבוה דשמואל says we estimate how much a person would want to be paid to have his hand cut off.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל's father said: we estimate how much a person would want to take to have his hand cut off.
steps.whatsHappening: אבוה דשמואל answers the question with a way to measure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He offers a concrete picture: imagine paying someone to let his hand be cut off. The גמרא will now test whether this really measures only pain.

phrases.english: שמואל's father said:
We estimate how much a person would want to take
to have his hand cut off.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אֲבוּהּ דִּשְׁמוּאֵל אוֹמְדִין כַּמָּה אָדָם רוֹצֶה לִיטּוֹל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the שאלה of step 5
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Estimate how much a person would accept to have his hand cut off

steps.title: Cutting off a hand involves all five payments, not just pain
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that losing a hand includes all five payments, so the estimate does not isolate pain.
steps.simpleTranslation: To have his hand cut off?! That is not pain alone. All five things are there!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks אבוה דשמואל's method. Cutting off a hand brings much more than pain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Losing a hand means damage, pain, medical costs, lost work and embarrassment. The price someone would ask would cover all of these. So it cannot tell us the value of pain alone, which was the whole question.

keyTerms.meaning: The five payments: נזק, צער, ריפוי, שבת, בושת

phrases.english: To have his hand cut off?!
It is not pain alone —
all five things are there!

steps.triggerLanguage: לִקְטוֹעַ לוֹ יָדוֹ לָא צַעַר לְחוֹדֵיהּ הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges אבוה דשמואל's method from step 6
steps.kashyaTarget: The estimate based on cutting off a healthy hand
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The price would include all five payments, so it does not isolate צער

steps.title: No sane person would sell his hand
steps.stepSummary: A second objection: only fools would take money to lose a hand, so the estimate makes no sense.
steps.simpleTranslation: And furthermore, are we dealing with fools?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a second problem with the same method. A normal person would never agree to this at any price.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An estimate only works if a reasonable person would name a price. Nobody sensible sells his hand, so the question has no real answer. The method cannot be used in practice.

phrases.english: And furthermore, are we dealing with fools?!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְעוֹד בְּשׁוּפְטָנֵי עָסְקִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second objection to the same method
steps.kashyaTarget: The estimate based on cutting off a healthy hand
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: No reasonable person would accept money for this, so no real price can be found

steps.title: A hand that is already severed
steps.stepSummary: The method is revised: estimate what a person would take to have an already severed, useless hand cut off.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather: to cut off his severed hand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the method so it avoids both objections.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A hand that is already severed is useless. Cutting it off causes no loss of use, no lost work, and a normal person might agree for a price. So the price should reflect mainly the pain.
steps.confusionAlert: "Severed hand" here means a hand that is still attached but already useless. That is why cutting it off would still hurt.

phrases.english: Rather: to cut off his already severed hand.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא לִקְטוֹעַ יָדוֹ הַקְּטוּעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objections in steps 7 and 8 by changing the case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Estimating the loss of a healthy hand mixes in all five payments and is unrealistic
steps.terutzMaskana: Estimate the loss of a useless hand, which leaves mainly pain

steps.title: Even a useless hand brings embarrassment
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that even cutting off a useless hand involves בושת as well as pain.
steps.simpleTranslation: With his severed hand too, there is not pain alone. There is pain and embarrassment, because it is shameful to him to have flesh taken from him and thrown to the dogs.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the revised method. Even this case does not isolate pain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person feels ashamed to have part of his body cut off and thrown away, even a useless part. So the price would include בושת along with צער. The method still does not measure pain alone, and the גמרא will need a better case.

keyTerms.meaning: Embarrassment, one of the five payments
The matter is shameful to him
To throw it to the dogs

steps.whatToRemember: The goal is to find a case that measures pain alone. A healthy hand brings in all five payments, and a useless hand still brings in בושת. The search for a clean method continues.

phrases.english: His severed hand too —
there is not pain alone,
there is pain and embarrassment —
because it is a shameful matter for him
to take from his flesh and throw it to the dogs!

steps.triggerLanguage: יָדוֹ הַקְּטוּעָה נָמֵי לָא צַעַר לְחוֹדֵיהּ אִיכָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the revised method of step 9
steps.kashyaTarget: The estimate based on cutting off an already severed hand
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Losing even a useless body part is shameful, so the price includes בושת and does not isolate צער

steps.title: A hand the government already ordered cut off: drug versus sword
steps.stepSummary: To remove the problem of בושת, the גמרא changes the case to a hand the government has already ordered cut off. The only open question is the method: a painless drug or a painful sword.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, we estimate how much a person would want to take to have his hand cut off when the government has already decreed it, going from a drug to a sword.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the בושת problem from Step 10 with a new case. The hand will be cut off no matter what, so the only difference left is pain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The hand is going to be removed anyway by government order, so there is no new loss of the hand and no new shame. The only difference between a drug and a sword is how much it hurts. So the amount a person would accept to switch from the drug to the sword measures pain alone.

keyTerms.meaning: written down by the government, meaning already decreed to be cut off
a drug that removes the limb without pain

phrases.english: Rather, we estimate how much a person
would want to take to have his hand cut off
which is written down by the government,
phrases.notes: The government has already ordered this hand removed, so it is going to happen anyway.

phrases.english: going from a drug to a sword.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אוֹמְדִין כַּמָּה אָדָם רוֹצֶה לִיטּוֹל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the בושת objection of Step 10 by changing the case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case so that only one factor, pain, is left
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Cutting off even a useless hand also involves shame, so the measure is mixed.
steps.terutzMaskana: If the hand is already condemned, only the method differs, and that difference is pure pain.

steps.title: Nobody would take money to suffer
steps.stepSummary: The objection: here too, no sane person would accept money to be cut with a sword instead of a drug.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say: Here too, a person would not take money and cause himself pain!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the new method with the same kind of problem it raised in Step 8. No normal person would accept money to suffer more.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The method still asks what someone would 'take' to accept pain. A normal person refuses at any price, so the question has no real answer.

phrases.english: They say: here too,
a person would not take money and cause himself pain!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי: הָכָא נָמֵי לָא שָׁקֵיל וּמְצַעַר נַפְשֵׁיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the method of Step 11.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Asking what a person would accept in order to suffer more gives no real number, because nobody would agree.

steps.title: Flip it: what would he pay to get the drug instead of the sword
steps.stepSummary: The final method: estimate how much a person would pay to switch from the sword to the painless drug.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, we estimate how much a person would want to give to have his condemned hand cut off going from a sword to a drug.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא flips the question around. Instead of asking what he would take to suffer, it asks what he would pay to avoid suffering.
steps.deeperAnalysis: People really do pay to avoid pain, so this question has a real answer. The amount he would pay to avoid the sword is the value of the pain, and the injurer pays that.
steps.whatToRemember: The final measure of צער: how much a person would pay to have his already-condemned hand removed by a painless drug instead of a sword.

phrases.english: Rather, we estimate how much a person
would want to give to have his hand cut off
which is written down by the government,
going from a sword to a drug.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אוֹמְדִין כַּמָּה אָדָם רוֹצֶה לִיתֵּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 12 by reversing the direction of the estimate.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We ask what he would accept to suffer, which nobody would do.
steps.terutzMaskana: We ask what he would pay to avoid suffering, which people really do.

steps.title: But the משנה says 'take', not 'give'
steps.stepSummary: The new method uses 'give,' but the משנה's wording says 'take.'
steps.simpleTranslation: This word 'to take'?! It should have said 'to give'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא checks the new method against the words of the משנה and finds a mismatch.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה measures צער by how much a person 'would want to take.' If the method is really about what he would pay, the משנה should have said 'to give.'

phrases.english: This word, 'to take'?!
phrases.notes: This is the word in our משנה about measuring pain: how much a person 'would want to take.'

phrases.english: It should have said 'to give'!

steps.triggerLanguage: הַאי לִיטּוֹל לִיתֵּן מִבְּעֵי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges Step 13 using the wording of the משנה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה's word 'take' does not fit a method built on what the victim would pay.

steps.title: He takes from the injurer what he himself would have given
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע explains that 'take' means the victim takes from the injurer the amount he would have paid.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא son of רב יהושע said: This one takes from that one what this one would have given.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע explains the משנה's wording so that it fits the 'give' method.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both words are correct. The victim 'takes' money from the injurer, and the amount is set by what the victim would have 'given' to avoid the pain.

keyTerms.meaning: this one from that one: the victim from the injurer

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה's 'take' refers to what the victim collects, and the amount equals what he would have paid to avoid the pain.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ:
phrases.english: רב הונא son of רב יהושע said:
This one takes from that one,
phrases.notes: 'This one' is the injured man, and 'that one' is the man who hurt him.

phrases.english: what this one would have given.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ: לִיטּוֹל זֶה מִזֶּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 14's wording problem.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Take' means the victim's own willingness to accept money.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Take' means what he collects from the injurer, measured by what he would have given.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה on medical costs
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא moves to the next payment, ריפוי, by quoting the משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Medical costs: If he struck him, he must heal him, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes with צער and opens the topic of ריפוי. It is setting up the ברייתא that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says the injurer must pay to heal the victim. The ברייתא that follows will define how far that duty goes.

keyTerms.meaning: medical costs, one of the five payments
to heal him, meaning to pay for his treatment

phrases.english: Medical costs: if he struck him,
he is obligated to heal him, and so on.

steps.triggerLanguage: רִפּוּי הִכָּהוּ חַיָּיב לְרַפּאוֹתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from צער to the next payment.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who injures must pay to heal the victim.

steps.title: A reopened wound: is the injurer still responsible?
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that if growths caused by the injury reopen the wound, the injurer pays again for healing and lost work. If the growths came from another cause, he does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Our Rabbis taught: If growths came up because of the wound and the wound reopened, he must heal him and pay for his lost work. If not because of the wound, he need not heal him or pay for his lost work.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that sets a limit on the duty to pay for healing. The injurer pays only for problems his blow caused.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the growths came from the injury, the reopened wound is still the injurer's fault, so he pays ריפוי and שבת again. If the growths have some other cause, the new problem is not his doing, so he owes nothing for it.
steps.whatToRemember: The injurer pays for healing and lost work only when the new problem comes from his blow.

phrases.english: Our Rabbis taught:
phrases.notes: The standard printed גמרא doesn't have these words; the square brackets show the corrected wording adds them.

phrases.english: If growths came up on it because of the wound,
and the wound reopened,
he is obligated to heal him,
and obligated to pay him for his lost work.
If not because of the wound,
he is not obligated to heal him,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵינוֹ חַיָּיב לִיתֵּן לוֹ דְּמֵי שִׁבְתּוֹ.
phrases.english: and not obligated to pay him for his lost work.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: עָלוּ בּוֹ צְמָחִים מֵחֲמַת הַמַּכָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא that spells out the limits of the משנה's rule of ריפוי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Growths caused by the injury: the injurer pays healing and lost work. Growths from another cause: he pays nothing for them.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: pay for healing but not for lost work
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues with רבי יהודה's view: even when the growths come from the injury, the injurer pays for healing but not for lost work.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: even if the growths came because of the injury, the injurer must pay to heal him, but he does not have to pay for his lost work.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps quoting the same ברייתא from step 17. Now רבי יהודה gives his opinion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first view said that when the growths come from the injury, the injurer pays both healing and lost work again. רבי יהודה splits the two payments: healing yes, lost work no. That split is what the rest of the sugya will try to explain.

keyTerms.meaning: lost work time, loss of livelihood

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
even if [the growths came] because of the injury,
phrases.notes: He is talking about the growths from step 17 that reopened the wound.

phrases.english: he is liable to heal him,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵינוֹ חַיָּיב לִיתֵּן לוֹ דְּמֵי שִׁבְתּוֹ.
phrases.english: but he is not liable to give him the value of his lost work.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: אַף מֵחֲמַת הַמַּכָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second opinion in the same ברייתא, disagreeing with the first view in step 17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the growths come from the injury, the injurer pays for healing but not for lost work.

steps.title: The חכמים: healing and lost work always go together
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים say that שבת and ריפוי are linked. Whenever one is owed, the other is owed. Whenever one is not owed, the other is not owed either.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים say: the תורה puts "his lost work" and "his healing" together. So anyone who must pay for lost work must pay for healing, and anyone who does not have to pay for lost work does not have to pay for healing.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא ends with a third opinion, the חכמים. They reject רבי יהודה's idea of paying one payment without the other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים argue from the way the פסוק puts the two words side by side, so the two payments are a package deal. In this case, where there is no payment for lost work, there is also no payment for healing.
steps.confusionAlert: There are three opinions in this ברייתא: the first view (liable for both), רבי יהודה (healing only), and the חכמים (linked, so here neither). Do not mix up the first view with the חכמים at the end.

phrases.english: And the Sages say:
"his lost work — and his healing";
phrases.notes: These words come straight from the פסוק in שמות 21:19, where the two payments appear side by side.

phrases.english: whoever is liable for lost work is liable for healing,

phrases.aramaic: וְשֶׁאֵינוֹ חַיָּיב בְּשֶׁבֶת – אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב בְּרִיפּוּי.
phrases.english: and whoever is not liable for lost work is not liable for healing.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַחֲכָמִים אוֹמְרִים: שִׁבְתּוֹ וּרְפוּאָתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רבי יהודה by linking the two payments.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Healing and lost work are tied together. Either both are owed or neither is.

steps.title: What is the real disagreement?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what idea lies underneath the dispute in the ברייתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: About what do they disagree?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. It asks for the reason behind the split in the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is aimed mainly at רבי יהודה's surprising split between the first view and his own. If the growths came from the injury, why would the injurer pay one payment but not the other? The next step gives an answer.

phrases.english: About what do they disagree?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּמַאי קָא מִיפַּלְגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind the ברייתא just quoted.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The underlying principle that divides the first view and רבי יהודה.

steps.title: The study hall's answer: may a wound be bandaged?
steps.stepSummary: רבה reports that the scholars in רב's study hall said the dispute is whether one may bandage a wound. The רבנן allow it, so the injurer pays everything. רבי יהודה forbids it, so he pays only healing, because the פסוק repeats the word for healing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: I found the scholars sitting in רב's study hall, and they were saying that the dispute is about whether a wound may be bandaged. The רבנן hold that it may, so the injurer pays for everything. רבי יהודה holds that it may not. So for healing, which the פסוק repeats, the injurer is liable. For lost work, which the פסוק does not repeat, he is not liable.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה gives an answer that he heard from the scholars in the study hall. They tie the whole dispute to the question of bandaging a wound.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If bandaging is allowed, growths caused by the bandage still count as coming from the injury, so the injurer pays both payments. If bandaging is not allowed, the victim brought the growths on himself. Even so, רבי יהודה makes him pay healing because of the doubled phrase "ורפא ירפא", which adds an extra healing payment.

keyTerms.meaning: is given to, may be put in (a bandage)

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'רבנן' means the first view in the ברייתא (liable for both), not the חכמים at the end of the ברייתא.

phrases.english: Rabba said:
I found the scholars in the study hall of Rav
sitting and saying:
here they disagree about whether a wound may be bandaged –
the Rabbis hold: a wound may be bandaged.

phrases.aramaic: וְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה סָבַר: מַכָּה לֹא נִיתְּנָה לְאֶגֶד;
phrases.english: And Rabbi Yehuda holds: a wound may not be bandaged;
for healing, which the verse repeated – he is liable;
phrases.notes: The פסוק says "ורפא ירפא" (שמות 21:19), saying "heal" twice.

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁבֶת, דְּלָא תְּנָא בֵּיהּ קְרָא – לָא מִיחַיַּיב.
phrases.english: for lost work, which the verse did not repeat – he is not liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה: אַשְׁכַּחְתִּינְהוּ לְרַבָּנַן בְּבֵי רַב דְּיָתְבִי וְקָאָמְרִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 20.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The dispute is whether a wound may be bandaged. רבי יהודה's healing payment comes from the doubled פסוק.

steps.title: רבה's challenge: then healing should not be paid either
steps.stepSummary: רבה objects that if bandaging is forbidden, the injurer should not owe even the healing payment.
steps.simpleTranslation: And I said to them: if a wound may not be bandaged, then he should not be liable for healing either!
steps.whatsHappening: רבה tells us that he challenged the explanation from the study hall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the victim did something forbidden by bandaging, the new damage is his own fault. Then there is no reason the injurer should pay anything for it, even healing. The doubled פסוק cannot make someone pay for damage the victim caused himself.

phrases.english: And I said to them:
if a wound may not be bandaged,
he should not be liable for healing either!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמֵינָא לְהוּ אֲנָא: אִי מַכָּה לֹא נִיתְּנָה לְאֶגֶד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the study hall's explanation of רבי יהודה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that רבי יהודה forbids bandaging but still makes the injurer pay for healing.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Damage caused by the victim's own forbidden action should not lead to any payment at all, so the healing payment makes no sense.

steps.title: Everyone allows a bandage, but not an excessive one
steps.stepSummary: רבה offers his own explanation. Everyone agrees a wound may be bandaged, but not with an excessive bandage.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, everyone agrees that a wound may be bandaged, but it may not be wrapped in an excessive bandage.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה replaces the study hall's explanation with his own. Both sides agree on the basic rule about bandaging.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Bandaging a wound normally is allowed by all. What is not allowed is overdoing it with an excessive bandage. The dispute is now framed around that extra, excessive bandage instead of bandaging in general, which avoids רבה's challenge.
steps.whatToRemember: רבה's conclusion: all agree a wound may be bandaged, but not with an excessive bandage. The study hall's idea that bandaging itself is the point of dispute was rejected.

phrases.english: Rather, according to everyone –
a wound may be bandaged,
but it may not be put in an excessive bandage.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא מַכָּה נִיתְּנָה לְאֶגֶד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves רבה's own challenge by reframing the dispute.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reframing the dispute: both sides agree on the basic rule, and the question shifts to excessive bandaging.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The dispute was thought to be whether bandaging is allowed at all.
steps.terutzMaskana: Everyone allows a normal bandage, and nobody allows an excessive one.

steps.title: Why רבי יהודה makes the injurer pay for healing but not lost work
steps.stepSummary: Since an excessive bandage is not allowed, רבי יהודה says the injurer pays ריפוי, which the פסוק repeats, but not שבת, which it does not repeat.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה holds: since a wound may not be wrapped in an excessive bandage, the injurer is liable for healing, which the verse repeated, but not for lost work, which the verse did not repeat.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה continues his own explanation and shows how רבי יהודה's ruling fits his new framework.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The victim could not have prevented the wound from reopening, because an extra-strong bandage is not allowed. So the injurer is still connected to the new damage. But רבי יהודה only adds the payment the פסוק stresses twice, which is healing.

keyTerms.meaning: The verse repeated it (said it twice)

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda holds:
since a wound may not be given an excessive bandage,
for healing, which the verse repeated, he is liable,
phrases.notes: The repeat is ״וְרַפֹּא יְרַפֵּא״ in שמות 21:19, which uses the word for healing twice.

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁבֶת דְּלָא תְּנָא בֵּיהּ קְרָא – לָא מִיחַיַּיב.
phrases.english: for lost work, which the verse did not repeat, he is not liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה סָבַר: כֵּיוָן דְּלֹא נִיתְּנָה לְאֶגֶד יְתֵירָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies רבה's framework from step 23 to רבי יהודה's view.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The dispute was thought to be about whether bandaging is allowed at all.
steps.terutzMaskana: Bandaging is allowed, an excessive bandage is not, and רבי יהודה adds only the doubled payment of ריפוי.

steps.title: Why the רבנן make him pay for lost work too
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן say that once the פסוק repeats ריפוי, שבת is owed as well, since the two are linked in the same פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis hold: since the verse repeated healing, he is also liable for lost work, which is linked to healing.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה now explains the רבנן's side inside the same framework.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן agree that the doubled healing word adds payment for the reopened wound. They go further: שבת sits right next to ריפוי in the פסוק, so whatever applies to one applies to the other.

keyTerms.meaning: It is linked by a היקש (placed side by side in the verse)

phrases.english: And the Rabbis hold:
since the verse repeated healing,
he is also liable for lost work,
which is linked to healing.
phrases.notes: In the פסוק, ״שִׁבְתּוֹ יִתֵּן״ and ״וְרַפֹּא יְרַפֵּא״ come right next to each other.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבָּנַן סָבְרִי: כֵּיוָן דִּתְנָא בֵּיהּ קְרָא בְּרִיפּוּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the other side of the dispute in the same framework.
steps.terutzMaskana: The רבנן extend the doubled ריפוי to שבת because the פסוק links them.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רבה, both sides agree a normal bandage is allowed and an excessive one is not, and both make the injurer pay ריפוי because the פסוק repeats it. They only argue over whether שבת rides along with ריפוי.

steps.title: Why רבי יהודה does not accept the link
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה rejects the link to שבת because the Torah limited it with the word ״רק״.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יהודה holds he is not liable for lost work, because the Merciful One limited it with the word ״רק״ (only).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers a question it does not spell out: why doesn't רבי יהודה accept the link between שבת and ריפוי?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה reads ״רק״, which is placed right before ״שִׁבְתּוֹ יִתֵּן״, as a limiting word. It cuts שבת out of this case even though the two payments are linked.

keyTerms.meaning: The Merciful One, meaning the Torah

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yehuda holds:
he is not liable for lost work,
because the Merciful One limited it with "only."
phrases.notes: שמות 21:19: ״רַק שִׁבְתּוֹ יִתֵּן״.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה סָבַר: שֶׁבֶת לָא מִיחַיַּיב, דְּמַעֲטֵיהּ רַחֲמָנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends רבי יהודה against the link the רבנן relied on in step 25.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A limiting word in the פסוק overrides the link
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The link should force רבי יהודה to require שבת as well.
steps.terutzMaskana: ״רק״ limits שבת, so the link does not apply here.

steps.title: How the רבנן use the word ״רק״
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן say ״רק״ only excludes growths that did not come from the injury.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the Rabbis say: ״רק״ comes to exclude growths that are not because of the wound.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what the רבנן learn from ״רק״, since they do not use it the way רבי יהודה does.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For the רבנן, ״רק״ still limits something, just something smaller. If growths come from an unrelated cause, the injurer owes nothing for them. Growths caused by the wound stay fully his responsibility.

keyTerms.meaning: Not because of the wound; from some other cause
That is what it comes to teach

phrases.english: And the Rabbis: "only"
comes for a case that is not because of the wound.
phrases.notes: He means it comes to exclude growths with another cause, so the injurer is free from paying for those.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבָּנַן – ״רַק״, לְשֶׁלֹּא מֵחֲמַת הַמַּכָּה הוּא דַּאֲתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that the רבנן also read ״רק״, but apply it to a different case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redirecting the limiting word to a different case
steps.terutzMaskana: For the רבנן, ״רק״ excludes only damage not caused by the wound.
steps.whatToRemember: Both sides use ״רק״. רבי יהודה uses it to remove שבת. The רבנן use it to remove growths that have nothing to do with the wound.

steps.title: What do the later רבנן do with the doubled healing word?
steps.stepSummary: The later רבנן say שבת and ריפוי always go together, so why does the פסוק repeat ריפוי?
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to the later Rabbis, who say that whoever is liable for lost work is liable for healing, and whoever is not liable for lost work is not liable for healing, why do I need the verse's repeat of healing?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the later רבנן from step 19. If the two payments always go together, the doubled word for healing seems to teach nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה used the repeat to add ריפוי alone, and the first רבנן used it to cover the reopened wound. The later רבנן never let ריפוי stand apart from שבת, so they seem to have no use for the extra word.

keyTerms.meaning: The later Rabbis (the last opinion in the ברייתא)

phrases.english: And according to the later Rabbis, who say:
whoever is liable for lost work is liable for healing,

phrases.aramaic: וְכֹל שֶׁאֵינוֹ חַיָּיב בְּשֶׁבֶת – אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב בְּרִיפּוּי;
phrases.english: and whoever is not liable for lost work is not liable for healing;

phrases.aramaic: רִיפּוּי דִּתְנָא בֵּיהּ קָרָא – לְמָה לִי?
phrases.english: the verse's repeat of healing, why do I need it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְרַבָּנַן בָּתְרָאֵי, דְּאָמְרִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from רבי יהודה and the first רבנן to the third opinion.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view of the later רבנן (step 19)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If שבת and ריפוי are always tied together, the doubled word for ריפוי has nothing left to teach.

steps.title: A doctor is given permission to heal
steps.stepSummary: The later רבנן use the doubled word for the teaching of the school of רבי ישמעאל: a doctor is allowed to heal.
steps.simpleTranslation: They need it for what the school of רבי ישמעאל taught. As it is taught: the school of רבי ישמעאל says: "and he shall surely heal"—from here we learn that permission is given to a doctor to heal.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. The later רבנן use the doubled word for a different lesson.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The repeat does not add a payment for them. It teaches that healing people is allowed, and that a doctor is not wrongly interfering with what ה׳ decided.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the classic source in the גמרא that practicing medicine is allowed.

phrases.aramaic: מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ לְכִדְתָנָא דְּבֵי רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל –
phrases.english: They need it for what the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught,
as it is taught: the school of Rabbi Yishmael says:
"and he shall surely heal"
phrases.notes: שמות 21:19

phrases.english: from here, that permission is given to a doctor to heal.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ לְכִדְתָנָא דְּבֵי רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 28.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The extra word is used for a different teaching
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The doubled word seemed useless for the later רבנן.
steps.terutzMaskana: It teaches that a doctor has permission to heal.

steps.title: Growths from the wound reopen it, and the injurer pays again
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that if growths caused by the wound reopen it, the injurer again owes ריפוי and שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: From where do we know that if growths came up because of the wound and the wound reopened, he must heal him and must give him his lost work? The verse says: "Only he shall pay for his lost work, and he shall surely heal."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא that states the rule for a wound that reopens.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This follows the first opinion we saw: when the reopening comes from the original wound, the injurer pays both ריפוי and שבת again. The source is the same פסוק that mentions both payments.

phrases.english: The Sages taught: From where do we know

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאִם עָלוּ בּוֹ צְמָחִים מֵחֲמַת הַמַּכָּה
phrases.english: that if growths came up on him because of the wound
and the wound reopened,
that he must heal him,
and must give him his lost work?

phrases.aramaic: תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: ״רַק שִׁבְתּוֹ יִתֵּן, וְרַפֹּא יְרַפֵּא״.
phrases.english: The verse teaches: "Only he shall pay for his lost work, and he shall surely heal."

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: מִנַּיִן שֶׁאִם עָלוּ בּוֹ צְמָחִים מֵחֲמַת הַמַּכָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new ברייתא that lays out the readings of ״רק״ discussed above.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If growths caused by the wound reopen it, the injurer again pays ריפוי and שבת.

steps.title: Growths from another cause are not covered
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא uses ״רק״ to exclude growths that did not come from the wound.
steps.simpleTranslation: One might think this applies even if the growths are not because of the wound. The verse says: "Only."
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא sets a limit on the rule it just taught.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is exactly how the רבנן read ״רק״ in step 27. Damage from an unrelated cause is not the injurer's responsibility.

phrases.english: One might think even when it is not because of the wound?
The verse teaches: "Only."

steps.triggerLanguage: יָכוֹל אֲפִילּוּ שֶׁלֹּא מֵחֲמַת הַמַּכָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the rule of step 30.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Growths not caused by the wound do not obligate the injurer.

steps.title: רבי יוסי בר יהודה exempts the injurer even for growths from the wound
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי בר יהודה reads ״רק״ more broadly and exempts the injurer even when the growths came from the wound.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי בר יהודה says: even if it is because of the wound he is exempt, as it says: "Only."
steps.whatsHappening: A second תנא disagrees with the first opinion in the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יוסי בר יהודה, ״רק״ limits the payment so much that a reopened wound is never charged again, even when the original injury caused it. He reads ״רק״ as excluding much more than the first opinion does.

keyTerms.meaning: Exempt, does not have to pay
As it is said (in the פסוק)

steps.whatToRemember: There are three readings of ״רק״. The רבנן: it excludes only unrelated growths. רבי יהודה: it removes שבת. רבי יוסי בר יהודה: it exempts the injurer even for growths caused by the wound.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda says:
even when it is because of the wound, he is exempt,
as it is said: "Only."

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: אַף מֵחֲמַת הַמַּכָּה פָּטוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the first opinion in the ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The injurer is exempt even when growths caused by the wound reopen it.

steps.title: First version: רבי יוסי בר יהודה exempts the injurer completely
steps.stepSummary: One version says רבי יוסי בר יהודה's exemption is total, both from ריפוי and from שבת, matching the later רבנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say that when רבי יוסי בר יהודה said 'even when the growths came from the wound he is exempt,' he meant completely exempt, following the later רבנן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how far רבי יוסי בר יהודה's exemption goes. This first version says it is a full exemption from everything.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The later רבנן hold that שבת and ריפוי always go together. So if the injurer is exempt from one, he is exempt from the other too. This is why this version says he pays nothing at all.

keyTerms.meaning: The later רבנן, who hold שבת and ריפוי always go together

phrases.english: There are those who say
'Even if it was due to the wound, he is exempt'
phrases.notes: This is quoting רבי יוסי בר יהודה from the previous step.

phrases.english: means completely exempt,
like the later רבנן;

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how far the exemption from Step 32 reaches.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In this version, the injurer is fully exempt from both ריפוי and שבת for growths caused by the wound, following the later רבנן.

steps.title: Second version: exempt from lost work but still pays medical costs
steps.stepSummary: Another version says רבי יוסי בר יהודה exempts the injurer only from שבת, but he still owes ריפוי, following his father רבי יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Others say רבי יוסי בר יהודה meant he is exempt from paying for lost work, but must still pay for healing. Whose view is that? His father's.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second, narrower reading of רבי יוסי בר יהודה. It also names who this reading follows: his father, רבי יהודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה holds that ריפוי can be owed even where שבת is not owed. So in this version the son follows his father: the payment for lost work is cut, but the medical payment stays.
steps.whatToRemember: There are two versions of רבי יוסי בר יהודה. In one he is fully exempt, like the later רבנן. In the other he pays ריפוי but not שבת, like his father רבי יהודה.

phrases.english: And there are those who say
'Even if it was due to the wound, he is exempt'
means exempt from lost work, but liable for healing;
Like whom? Like his father.
phrases.notes: His father is רבי יהודה, who holds you can owe healing costs even when you don't owe for lost work.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different version from Step 33's reading.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In this version, the injurer is exempt from שבת but liable for ריפוי, following רבי יהודה.

steps.title: Why would a פסוק be needed to exempt growths not caused by the wound?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא: if the growths did not come from the wound at all, the exemption should be obvious without a פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: 'One might think he is liable even when the growths were not caused by the wound, so the פסוק says רק.' Do we really need a פסוק for growths that were not caused by the wound?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the ברייתא from Step 31. It asks why a פסוק is needed for something that seems obvious.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the growths have nothing to do with the injury, of course the injurer should not pay for them. Using the word ״רק״ to teach this looks like wasting a פסוק on something we already know.

phrases.english: The Master said:
phrases.notes: This is the ברייתא from Step 31.

phrases.english: One might think even if it was not due to the wound?
Therefore the verse says: 'Only.'
For something not due to the wound, a verse is needed?!

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁלֹּא מֵחֲמַת הַמַּכָּה בָּעֵי קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the ברייתא of Step 31 and challenges why it needs the word ״רק״.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's use of ״רק״ to exempt growths not caused by the wound
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An exemption for damage the injurer did not cause is obvious, so no פסוק should be needed.

steps.title: It means the victim ignored his doctor and ate sweets
steps.stepSummary: 'Not caused by the wound' means the victim broke his doctor's orders, ate sweets, and made the wound fester. Without the פסוק, we might have blamed the injurer.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say: what does 'not caused by the wound' mean? As a ברייתא teaches: if he ignored the doctor and ate honey or sweets, which are bad for a wound, and the wound festered, you might think the injurer must pay to heal it. So the פסוק says רק.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that 'not caused by the wound' does not mean something completely unrelated. It means the wound got worse because the victim did something harmful.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the wound itself did become worse, so we might have thought the injurer is still responsible, since it is his wound. The פסוק teaches that because the victim's own disobedience caused the harm, the injurer does not pay. That is why the פסוק is needed.

phrases.english: They say:
What does 'not due to the wound' mean?
As it is taught in a ברייתא:
One who went against the doctor's words

phrases.aramaic: וְאָכַל דְּבַשׁ אוֹ כׇּל מִינֵי מְתִיקָה,
phrases.english: and ate honey or any kind of sweet,
because honey and all kinds of sweets
are harmful to the wound;
and his wound developed גרגותני;
One might think the injurer must heal him?
Therefore the verse says: 'Only.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי: מַאי ״שֶׁלֹּא מֵחֲמַת הַמַּכָּה״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 35.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Not caused by the wound' meant growths with no connection to the injury, so no פסוק was needed.
steps.terutzMaskana: It means the wound got worse because the victim disobeyed his doctor. That is a real question, so the פסוק is needed to exempt the injurer.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows the injurer does not pay for harm the victim brings on himself by ignoring medical advice.

steps.title: What is גרגותני?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the unusual word גרגותני means.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is גרגותני?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops to ask the meaning of a hard word from the ברייתא. The answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not a challenge. It is a simple question about a word, so that we understand the case in the ברייתא.

phrases.english: What is 'גרגותני'?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי ״גַּרְגּוּתְנִי״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about a word used in Step 36.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of the word גרגותני

steps.title: אביי explains: rotting flesh, and how to treat it
steps.stepSummary: אביי says גרגותני is rotting flesh. Its remedy is ice plant, wax, and wine dregs.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: it is rotting flesh. What is its cure? Ice plant, wax, and wine dregs.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי explains the word, and then the גמרא also gives the cure for this condition.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The wound has started to rot, which is why it is so serious. The remedy is added as useful practical information. It does not change the הלכה.

keyTerms.meaning: A plant used as medicine (ice plant)

phrases.english: אביי said:
Rotting flesh.
What is its cure?
Ice plant, wax, and wine dregs.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: נָאתָא כְּרִיכְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 37.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: גרגותני is rotting flesh. It is treated with ice plant, wax, and wine dregs.

steps.title: The victim can refuse to be treated by the injurer himself
steps.stepSummary: If the injurer offers to be the doctor himself, the victim may refuse, saying he sees him like a lion lying in wait.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the injurer says, 'I will be your doctor,' the victim can answer, 'To me you are like a lion lying in wait.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new topic: rules about how the medical payment works. The first rule is that the victim does not have to accept treatment from the person who hurt him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone who already injured you cannot be trusted to care for you. So the victim may demand money for a different doctor instead of accepting treatment from the injurer.

phrases.english: And if he says to him:
'I am your doctor,'
phrases.notes: The injurer is offering to heal the victim himself, so that he doesn't have to pay a doctor.

phrases.english: he can say to him:
'You seem to me like a lion lying in wait.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי אֲמַר לֵיהּ: ״אָסְיָיךְ אֲנָא״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new group of rules about paying ריפוי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The victim may refuse treatment from the injurer himself.

steps.title: The victim can refuse a free doctor
steps.stepSummary: If the injurer offers a doctor who works for free, the victim may refuse, because a free doctor is worth nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the injurer says, 'I will bring a doctor who works for free,' the victim can answer, 'A free doctor is worth free, meaning nothing.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second rule about the medical payment. The injurer cannot avoid paying by sending a free doctor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A doctor who works without pay is assumed not to care enough about the patient. So the victim may demand a proper, paid doctor at the injurer's expense.
steps.whatToRemember: The injurer cannot cut costs on ריפוי. He can't treat the victim himself, and he can't send a free doctor. The victim is entitled to a real doctor paid for by the injurer.

phrases.english: And if he says to him:
'I will bring a doctor who works for free,'
phrases.notes: Some versions have בְּמַגָּן, the word in round brackets, instead of דְּמַגָּן. The meaning is the same.

phrases.english: he can say to him:
'A doctor for free'
'is worth free (nothing).'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי אֲמַר לֵיהּ: ״מַיְיתִינָא אָסְיָא דְּמַגָּן״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second rule in the same series as Step 39.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The victim may refuse a free doctor and demand a properly paid one.

steps.title: The victim may refuse a doctor from far away
steps.stepSummary: If the injurer offers a doctor from a distant place, the victim may refuse, because a far-away doctor is like a blind eye.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the injurer says, 'I will bring you a doctor from far away,' the victim can answer, 'A far-away doctor is a blind eye.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a third case where the victim may turn down the injurer's medical plan, this time a doctor who lives far away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A doctor who is not nearby cannot keep checking the wound, so problems get missed. The victim has a right to care that actually heals him, not just any doctor the injurer chooses.

keyTerms.meaning: A blind eye, something that does not see what is happening

phrases.english: And if he (the injurer) says:
"I will bring you a doctor from far away,"
he (the victim) can say to him:
"A far-away doctor is a blind eye."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי אָמַר מַיְיתִינָא לָךְ אָסְיָא רַחִיקָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of the victim's valid objections to the injurer's offers (after a self-appointed doctor and a free doctor).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The victim may refuse a distant doctor, since he cannot monitor the healing properly.

steps.title: The injurer may refuse to hand the victim cash for self-treatment
steps.stepSummary: If the victim asks for the money so he can arrange his own healing, the injurer may refuse, because the victim may be careless and end up costing him more.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the victim says, 'Give the money to me and I will heal myself,' the injurer can answer, 'You will be careless with yourself and take more from me.'
steps.whatsHappening: Now the roles flip: the victim makes an offer, and the גמרא says the injurer is allowed to refuse it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the victim holds the cash, he might skimp on care to keep the money. Then the wound gets worse, and the injurer, who is responsible for full healing, ends up paying more.

keyTerms.meaning: That one; here it refers to the victim
You will be careless with yourself

steps.confusionAlert: In this case the victim is the one speaking first, and the injurer is the one refusing. That is the opposite of the earlier cases.

phrases.english: And if that one says to him:
phrases.notes: "That one" is the injured person, who is now making the offer.

phrases.english: "Give [the money] to me myself,
and I will heal myself,"
he (the injurer) can say to him:
"You will be careless with yourself
and you will take more from me."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי אֲמַר לֵיהּ הַיְאךְ הַב לִי לְדִידִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Switches from the victim's objections to the injurer's objection to a victim's proposal.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The injurer may refuse to give the medical money directly to the victim for self-treatment.

steps.title: The injurer may refuse a fixed lump sum
steps.stepSummary: If the victim asks for a fixed amount for his healing, the injurer may refuse, because the victim will be even more careless and people will call the injurer a 'damaging ox'.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the victim says, 'Set a fixed sum for me,' the injurer can answer, 'All the more so you will be careless with yourself, and people will call me a damaging ox.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives one more offer from the victim, a fixed payment, and says the injurer can refuse this too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a fixed sum, the victim keeps whatever he does not spend, so he has an even stronger reason to skip treatment. If he never heals, people will see it and blame the injurer as a dangerous person, like an ox that harms.

keyTerms.meaning: Set a fixed amount for me
A damaging ox; a nickname for someone known to harm others

steps.whatToRemember: Medical care must actually heal the victim. Each side may block a plan that makes real healing less likely: the victim can refuse a bad doctor, and the injurer can refuse to just hand over cash.

phrases.english: And if he (the victim) says to him:
"Set a fixed amount for me,"
he (the injurer) can say to him:
"All the more so you will be careless with yourself,
and they will call me: 'A damaging ox.'"

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי אֲמַר לֵיהּ קוּץ לִי מִקָּץ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on step 42 with a stronger case (כל שכן) and adds a second reason, damage to the injurer's reputation.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The injurer may refuse a fixed lump-sum settlement for medical costs.

steps.title: All the extra payments are owed even along with damage
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that all the extra payments (צער, רפוי, שבת, בושת) are paid even when the injurer also pays for נזק.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: all of them are paid even in a case where damage is paid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic by quoting a ברייתא about combining the payments.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One might think that once the injurer pays for the permanent damage (נזק), that covers everything. The ברייתא says no: the other payments are added on top.

keyTerms.meaning: In a case where there is also damage

phrases.english: It was taught:
And all of them are paid where there is damage.
phrases.notes: "All of them" means pain, medical costs, lost work, and embarrassment, paid on top of the damage payment.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנָא וְכוּלָּן מִשְׁתַּלְּמִין בִּמְקוֹם נֶזֶק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the medical-care details and introduces a new rule about combining payments.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: צער, רפוי, שבת and בושת are all paid in addition to נזק.

steps.title: Asking for the source
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where we learn that these payments are owed along with נזק.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where do we know these things?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the source in the תורה for the ברייתא's rule. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule is not obvious, since one might assume the damage payment covers everything. So the גמרא wants a פסוק behind it.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know these things?

phrases.english: From where do we know these things?

steps.triggerLanguage: מְנָהָנֵי מִילֵּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the ברייתא in step 44.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source in the תורה that the extra payments are added to נזק.

steps.title: The source is 'פצע תחת פצע'
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד in the name of רבא says the פסוק 'פצע תחת פצע' teaches that צער is paid even where נזק is paid.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב זביד said in the name of רבא: The פסוק says, 'A wound for a wound,' to teach that pain is paid even where damage is paid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question with a פסוק that shows pain money is owed on top of damage money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא reads the phrase 'פצע תחת פצע' as teaching that צער is paid even when the injury also caused נזק. The next step challenges whether this phrase is free to teach that.

phrases.english: Rav Zevid said in the name of Rava,
The verse says:
"A wound for a wound"
phrases.notes: שמות 21:25

phrases.english: to give payment for pain where there is damage.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב זְבִיד מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרָבָא אָמַר קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 45.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'פצע תחת פצע' teaches that צער is paid even where נזק is paid.

steps.title: Challenge: the verse is needed for something else
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins to object that this פסוק is already needed to teach a different law.
steps.simpleTranslation: But this verse is needed for...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a challenge to רב זביד's source. The sentence continues on the next part of the daf, so this step only sets up the challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A פסוק can only teach a new law if it is not already being used for another lesson. The גמרא is about to claim 'פצע תחת פצע' is already busy with something else.

phrases.english: This [verse] is needed for...

steps.triggerLanguage: הַאי מִבְּעֵי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the source given in step 46.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב זביד's use of 'פצע תחת פצע' as the source for paying צער along with נזק.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the פסוק is already needed for another law, it cannot also serve as the source for this one.
